newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt sold at close on Australian weakness.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt sold at close on Australian weakness.

* NZ debt sold at Tuesday's close after promising start
* Australian retail sales rebound in January, shock market
* RBNZ economic forecasts the next key local driver
New Zealand yields gave up their early gains to coast to a poor finish on Tuesday, dragged higher by weakness in Australian bonds.

Australian retail sales rebounded in January and building approvals soared, cementing the market's fears of an accelerating economy. Traders had gone into the data short, and yields took a hammering on the back of the news.
Local bond yields suffered alongside their trans-tasman counterparts, although the extent of the weakness was limited.
Mid and long bonds finished five basis points above Monday's close, after putting in an impressive performance earlier in the day.
"It looked as though it was going to be quite constructive this morning, and it just didn't really happen," one dealer said.
In the money market, the 90-day bank bills climbed up to 7.72 percent after opening down at 7.65 percent, but were still slightly below their 7.76 percent close on Monday.

New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters delivered few surprises for the markets in the Budget Policy Statement, released in the early afternoon. A NZ$250 million fall in forecasted extra spending for the 1997-98 year was in line with expectations.
Peters reiterated that inflation pressures were still a risk in the economy, and said a fiscal easing was currently inappropriate.

"He keeps concentrating on the inflation story, housing and so on...it's the tone that's going to come out from the Reserve Bank as well, so it just reinforces the sentiment that's been around the last couple of weeks.
"Tight conditions are probably going to be the norm rather than the opposite," one dealer said.
The Reserve Bank is due to release its economic projections on March 13, the next key focus on the domestic front.
